cells.tense: You are here, holding several threads at once, and it is working.
cells.ask: Pick one piece of what your people share and say aloud what it is for. Simple words. No need to get it right.
cells.core:
You can hold several threads at once without dropping any, and you gather them into one course on purpose. It comes out as knowing what your group meant, what you've kept, why it still matters. Around a table or in a group thread the words land, and they land because you did the putting-together first.

What you have for the next step is fairness as a plain habit rather than a tally — you can give more than your half without turning it into a debt, and take what's handed to you without an apology. That is the part worth feeding. Keep the cost in view: this kind of balance doesn't stay put, and each exchange asks for the same choice again.
cells.sheetLine: You gather what the group means, and you can say it plainly.
cells.verb: turning scattered thoughts into one course and steering by it
cells.place: among the old sayings and the shared meanings a community keeps

cells.tense: You are ahead of them in your head, building the finished thing before any of it is here.
cells.ask: Write the current draft of the shared plan in three lines. Show it to one person. Change the lines only if they do.
cells.core:
You are running the gathering ahead of itself, rehearsing how the next one will go, what your group should decide, the exact words this will settle on. Several strands get woven into one plan in your head, and none of it is checked against the actual conversation. The collecting is aimed at a moment that hasn't happened.

That plan usually came from wanting to be close to these people, and that want is fine. But when it runs ahead of them, the direction stops coming from the actual conversation. Bring one collection back to the present. Only what the people in front of you actually say can adjust the course — not your picture of them.
cells.sheetLine: You've already decided what they'll agree to.
cells.verb: turning scattered thoughts into one course and steering by it
cells.place: among the old sayings and the shared meanings a community keeps

cells.tense: You stopped adding to what your people share a while back, and you are still standing where that stopped.
cells.ask: Add one line or one story to something your people are keeping. Say it badly. It counts as soon as they hear it.
cells.core:
You are part of something passed down, and lately you've been leaving the adding to the others. The threads it takes to make one shared thing are sitting loose, and you don't reach for them. The offering stopped, and the standing still is where you are now. What you know didn't go anywhere; the joining in did.

What is missing is not input and not another plan — it is the feeling of your own footing settling, being near these people without disappearing into them. That settles in one shared act, theirs with you. Let their move reach you first, then add your line to what's kept.
cells.sheetLine: You know what your people mean. You're not adding to it.
cells.verb: turning scattered thoughts into one course and steering by it
cells.place: among the old sayings and the shared meanings a community keeps

cells.tense: You are already sorting the shared thoughts into one story, and you talk about it as if the story sorted itself.
cells.ask: Tell one person 'this one's mine': the phrase your family picked up, or the thing you got the group to start doing.
cells.core:
You are already one of the people who decides what gets kept and what quietly stops. You keep multiples in order, decide what the group means, put it back out in words others repeat. And you describe it as just the way things work. It happens continuously; the saying-so doesn't.

The older thing sitting under this is plain joy when a group is in it together, loyalty underneath. Enough to claim the smallest part. One word to one person, in your own voice, naming what you decided: that is the acting from the original, not from a report of it.

cells.place: among the old sayings and the shared meanings a community keeps

attempts.check: The record is silent on how this person's culture actually treats them, so I cannot claim they are heard or unheard in their community; the reader could rightly say the people around them are fine and it is one setting that grates. The ask survives being wrong: it is a small spoken act, useful when the read is off. The sentence that serves me rather than them is 'You're the one deciding what gets carried — you just never called it that,' because it makes the stance sound settled when I do not know their standing at all.
